It mills wheat and maize at its Riverside mill, employing 26 workers and generating annual revenue of $2.4 million. Thornfen can finance the purchase by issuing 400,000 new ordinary shares to existing family shareholders at $1.50 each, raising $600,000, or by taking a $600,000 bank loan at 6% annual interest over 8 years, costing $36,000 in interest each year. However, the bank loan is likely quicker to arrange from a single known lender [k], while the 10-year debenture ties Hartcliffe to $140,000 a year and repayment of $2 million in year ten [app], which could strain cash flow if the aerospace contract milestones slip beyond March [an]. Overall, Hartcliffe should sell the debentures [eval], because protecting the family-built factory and saving $30,000 a year matter more than speed of arrangement [eval].

evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the family-built factory

scenario_stem:
Invermere Marine Plc is a public limited company listed on the Country X Stock Exchange, operating coastal freight and ferry services for 13 years. It employs 210 crew and staff and reported revenue of $21 million last year. Invermere wants $6 million for a 60-metre container vessel, expected to earn $1.5 million extra revenue a year. Ferry bookings have risen 12% since the new timetable began.

Invermere can raise the $6 million through a general issue of 3 million new ordinary shares at $2.00 each, or by borrowing $6 million for 10 years at a fixed 7.25%, costing $435,000 a year. The share issue would spread ownership across many new investors; the loan keeps ownership concentrated but fixes repayments for a decade. The shareholders vote on 25 October.

questions.question_text: Define 'long-term finance'.
questions.model_answer: Finance used for a period longer than one year, usually to fund capital projects and expansion rather than short-term needs [2].

knowledge_max_2: finance used for more than one year
suited to capital projects and long-term expansion

questions.question_text: Calculate the total interest Invermere would pay over 10 years on the $6 million loan at 7.25% a year.
questions.model_answer: Step 1: annual interest = $6,000,000 Ã— 7.25% [k] = $435,000 a year [app]. Step 2: total interest = $435,000 Ã— 10 years [k] = $4,350,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: annual interest = principal Ã— annual rate
total interest = annual interest Ã— number of years

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages to Invermere of borrowing $6 million at a fixed 7.25% for 10 years.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Interest is fixed and compulsory [k], so $435,000 must be paid each of the 10 years even if freight demand dips below revenue of $21 million [app], reducing profit available for dividends [an]. Problem 2: The $6 million itself must be repaid [k], so a decade of annual $435,000 interest is followed by one large capital repayment [app], straining liquidity in the tenth year [an].

knowledge_max_2: fixed interest must be paid every year regardless of performance
loans must be repaid in full at the end of the term
application_max_2: $435,000 a year at 7.25% on $6 million for 10 years
last year's revenue was $21 million
analysis_max_2: fixed costs reduce dividend capacity in weak years
the final repayment creates a large cash strain

questions.question_text: Do you think Invermere Marine Plc should borrow the $6 million rather than issue new ordinary shares? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Borrowing keeps ownership concentrated [k], and at a fixed 7.25% the $435,000 yearly cost is covered by the vessel's expected $1.5 million extra revenue, leaving over $1 million of headroom a year [app], so a decade of repayments is affordable without diluting current investors [an]. However, the share issue of 3 million new shares at $2.00 raises the same $6 million with no repayment ever [k], protecting Invermere if freight demand turns, though it would spread ownership across many new investors expecting future dividends on $21 million revenue [app], cutting existing shareholders' share [an]. Overall, Invermere should borrow the $6 million [eval], because the vessel's $1.5 million extra annual revenue comfortably covers the $435,000 interest while ownership stays concentrated [eval].

knowledge_max_2: borrowing preserves ownership but creates fixed repayments
share issue raises permanent capital but dilutes ownership
application_max_2: loan costs $435,000 a year at 7.25% versus $1.5 million expected extra revenue
3 million shares at $2.00 raise the same $6 million
analysis_max_2: affordability of fixed interest weighed against dilution
risk of demand falling versus permanent capital safety
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the vessel investment

scenario_stem:
Keswickmoor Ceramics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X founded 9 years ago, making ceramic tiles for hotels and restaurants. It employs 52 workers at its Moorcroft kilns, earned $4.6 million revenue last year, and holds $1.1 million of retained profit. Two national hotel chains have asked for 300,000 extra tiles next year. Keswickmoor wants $750,000 for a new glaze laboratory and automated kiln line.

The directors can take a $750,000 bank loan at 5.5% over 6 years ($41,250 a year interest) or issue 500,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 each to raise the same $750,000. The bank would give no further credit while the loan is outstanding. Keeping the glaze quality lead matters for its hotel clients. The board votes on 20 February.

questions.question_text: Define 'ordinary shares'.
questions.model_answer: The standard voting shares of a company, giving holders ownership rights and a claim to dividends from profit [2].

knowledge_max_2: ordinary shares carry ownership and voting rights
ordinary shareholders receive dividends from profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Keswickmoor might take the bank loan rather than issue new shares.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Existing shareholders keep full ownership [k], because no 500,000 new ordinary shares are added to the current holding [app]. Reason 2: Loan interest is certain and tax-deductible [k], at $41,250 a year for 6 years, reducing the tax payable on profits from $4.6 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: a bank loan does not change ownership or control
loan interest is certain in advance and tax-deductible
application_max_2: the share option would add 500,000 new ordinary shares
the loan costs $41,250 a year at 5.5% over 6 years

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Keswickmoor of issuing the 500,000 new ordinary shares at $1.50 each.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Shares are permanent capital [k], so the $750,000 raised never has to be repaid, unlike the loan due in full after 6 years [app], protecting cash flow while the glaze laboratory is built [an]. Advantage 2: No fixed interest [k], so dividends can fall if hotel orders below $4.6 million disappoint, whereas $41,250 a year interest would still fall due [app], giving flexibility in weak seasons [an].

knowledge_max_2: share capital is permanent and never has to be repaid
ordinary dividends can be reduced when profit falls
application_max_2: 500,000 shares at $1.50 each raise $750,000
the loan at 5.5% costs $41,250 a year for 6 years
analysis_max_2: no repayment protects cash during the laboratory build
flexible dividends give room in weak seasons

questions.question_text: Do you think Keswickmoor Ceramics Ltd should take the bank loan rather than issue new ordinary shares? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The bank loan raises $750,000 quickly [k], preserves full ownership and costs a tax-deductible $41,250 a year, so Keswickmoor keeps control while hotel clients get their extra 300,000 tiles [app], and the 5.5% rate is affordable against $4.6 million revenue [an]. However, issuing 500,000 new shares at $1.50 brings $750,000 that never needs repaying [k], avoids the clause that the bank gives no further credit while the loan is outstanding and shields the glaze laboratory project if demand dips [app], reducing fixed obligations across the 6 years [an]. Overall, Keswickmoor should issue the new ordinary shares [eval], because the no-further-credit clause would cramp growth, making permanent share capital the safer route despite the $1.50 dilution [eval].

knowledge_max_2: bank loans are quick, tax-deductible and preserve ownership
share issue raises permanent capital with no repayment obligation
application_max_2: loan costs $41,250 a year at 5.5% for 6 years; shares at $1.50 raise $750,000
two national hotel chains want 300,000 extra tiles; revenue was $4.6 million
analysis_max_2: speed and control weighed against the no-further-credit clause
permanent capital versus fixed annual obligations
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the figures and the hotel-chain order
